evidence_items.explanation: The report records preference for GPT-4 on 70.2% of 5,214 prompts and broad benchmark gains over predecessors. These are developer-run evaluations supporting a substantial capability and response-quality advance, not proof of human understanding.

The authors report experiments across mathematics, coding, vision, medicine, law, and psychology. Because they examined an early development version, this corroborates the capability direction but is not treated as a matched evaluation of the released model.
The study reports predictable relationships between language-model loss, model size, data, and compute. It supports the general scaling rationale but does not isolate why GPT-4 improved.

The study found that a 70-billion-parameter model trained on more data outperformed several larger models. This qualifies a parameter-count-only reading of bigger means better; it does not contradict improvement from jointly scaling resources.

unresolved_gaps: The evidence does not isolate scaling's causal contribution from data selection, training methods, and alignment.
Human response preference is not a direct measurement of human indistinguishability.
